summary: Cellular networks migrating to IPv6 face prefix management issues. This informational RFC proposes using DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation so an access router can offload the delegation and release of prefixes to a DHCPv6 server, in LTE networks.

plainLanguage.summary: A hotel front desk used to hand out every room key. This hands that job to a back-office clerk to free up the desk.

questions: how is dhcpv6 prefix delegation used in lte
how do cellular networks manage ipv6 prefixes
how does dhcpv6 prefix delegation work in lte networks
what is the difference between stateless and stateful address configuration
how are ipv6 prefixes released when devices disconnect
subtitle: How cellular networks delegate IPv6 address blocks to mobile devices using standard DHCP.

tldr.problem: LTE and other cellular networks need to assign IPv6 prefixes to mobile devices, but unlike fixed networks, cellular links are point-to-point and many devices connect at once. Traditional methods do not scale well for the number of simultaneous connections.
tldr.mechanism: DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (DHCP-PD) allows the access router to request blocks of IPv6 prefixes from a central DHCP server. The router then delegates parts of those prefixes to mobile devices on demand. Authentication servers (RADIUS or Diameter) can also provide prefix information.
tldr.outcome: DHCPv6-PD became a standard practice in cellular networks, enabling scalable prefix management without requiring the access router to track and manage pools of prefixes internally.

today: RFC 6653 is Informational and describes practices that have been widely adopted in cellular networks. DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation is a standard part of LTE and 5G IPv6 deployment.

sections.title: The Prefix Management Problem in LTE
sections.content:
LTE (Long-Term Evolution) and other cellular networks are migrating to IPv6. In these networks, each mobile device gets a direct connection to an access router (the PDN Gateway in LTE), and each connection is point-to-point. In this model, each mobile device needs its own IPv6 prefix, not just an address.

When an access router manages IPv6 prefixes directly, it must track which prefixes are in use, which are free, and when to release them as devices disconnect. As the number of mobile devices grows, this internal management becomes complex and does not scale. The problem is especially acute because mobile devices attach and detach frequently, and many devices may attach simultaneously.

The solution is to offload prefix management to a centralized DHCPv6 server, which can keep track of prefix pools and allocations across many access routers.

sections.title: How DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation Works
sections.content:
DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (DHCPv6-PD, defined in RFC 3633) allows a DHCP client to request a block of IPv6 prefixes, not just addresses. In the cellular network scenario, the access router acts as the DHCP client (called the Requesting Router) and requests prefixes from a DHCP server (called the Delegating Router).

When a mobile device attaches, the access router sends a DHCP Solicit message requesting a prefix with the desired length (for example, a /64 prefix). The DHCP server responds with an Advertise message offering available prefixes. The router then sends a Request message, and the server sends a Reply with the delegated prefix. The router stores the prefix and uses it to assign addresses to the mobile device, either via stateless address autoconfiguration or by running a DHCP server locally for the mobile device.
sections.plainLanguage: The desk clerk calls the manager: "I need keys for five new guests." The manager says, "Here is a batch of twenty keys." The clerk hands them out as guests arrive.

sections.title: Stateless and Stateful Address Configuration
sections.content:
After the access router receives a prefix from the DHCP server, it can configure the mobile device's address in two ways. In stateless configuration, the router sends a Router Advertisement message with the prefix information. The mobile device then generates its own address by appending a random suffix to the prefix, following RFC 4861 (IPv6 Neighbor Discovery).

In stateful configuration, the access router runs a DHCP server locally. The mobile device sends a DHCP Solicit message to the router, which responds with a specific address from the prefix it received. This approach gives the network operator more control over which addresses are assigned.

Both approaches can coexist in the same network: the access router requests a shorter prefix (such as /48) from the DHCP server, then delegates /64 subnets from that range to mobile devices.

sections.title: Releasing Prefixes When Devices Disconnect
sections.content:
When a mobile device detaches (powers off, moves away, or hands over to another network), the prefixes assigned to it must be released so they can be reused by other devices. Release happens in two ways. First, the access router can send a DHCP Release message to the DHCP server, explicitly returning the prefixes. Second, prefixes can age out: the DHCP server assigns a lifetime to each prefix (communicated via DHCP and Router Advertisement options), and the prefix becomes invalid when the lifetime expires.

The RFC notes that when a device becomes idle (no longer actively communicating), the access router should not release the prefix if the device may wake up and use it again. This is managed through the lifetime mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: When a guest checks out, the clerk either calls the manager to return the room key, or waits for the key to expire (the manager notes that the clerk has not used that key for a month, so it can be given to someone else).

sections.title: Integration with Authentication and Accounting
sections.content:
Cellular networks use RADIUS and Diameter protocols for authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA). These systems can also play a role in prefix management. When a mobile device authenticates, an AAA server can provide prefix information via the Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attribute. The DHCP server can query the AAA server to learn what prefixes a particular device should receive, integrating prefix allocation with the network's subscriber management and billing systems.

RFC 4818 defines the Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attribute for use with both RADIUS and Diameter. This allows carriers to manage prefix allocations alongside subscription policies and service tiers.
sections.plainLanguage: When a guest checks in, the front desk calls the manager, who checks the guest's reservation and says, "Give this guest rooms 200-210." That way, different guests get different room sets based on their booking.
